passage: I used to think the best thing to do when a friend cried was to fix it. When Afreen's mother was ill, I found Jagdish crying in the office pantry, and I said, "Do not cry, it will be okay." He cried harder, turned away and said he was fine. I felt useless. I am Afreen, and I went home thinking about it. The next time, with a different friend, I said nothing at first. I put a tissue nearby, sat with her and asked softly, "Would you like me to stay, or would you like space?" She wanted me to stay. We sat there. I think crying does not always need fixing; it needs someone who does not rush it.

qa.q: Where did Afreen find Jagdish crying?
qa.a: Afreen found Jagdish crying in the office pantry.

qa.q: Why did Afreen feel useless after telling Jagdish not to cry?
qa.a: Afreen saw that the words made the crying worse and did not comfort. The reason may have been that Jagdish needed room to feel, not reassurance.

qa.q: What did Afreen do differently with the next friend?
qa.a: Afreen stayed quiet, put a tissue nearby, sat beside her and asked whether she wanted company or space.

qa.q: How might Jagdish have felt when told not to cry?
qa.a: Jagdish probably felt hurried or unheard, since the crying got harder and the reply turned to "I am fine".

grounding: Reflective account of a young adult learning to support a crying friend with a tissue, quiet presence and asking what would help.

passage: Counsellor's note, Wednesday. I am Lalit, the youth counsellor. During a walk-in visit, Santosh began to cry while describing a failed exam. A volunteer beside him started to say, "Stop, do not cry, it is only an exam," and Santosh went quiet and wiped his face. I gently asked the volunteer to sit back. I put a box of tissues on the table and said, "Take your time." After a while Santosh said he wanted to talk. I asked, "What would help right now?" He said, "Just listen." I noted that not rushing him made the difference. I will remind volunteers that a cry does not always need fixing. I will check on Santosh next week.

qa.q: What did Lalit put on the table?
qa.a: Lalit put a box of tissues on the table.

qa.q: What did Santosh's going quiet after "Stop" suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggested he felt hurried or dismissed and shut down, though he might also simply have been embarrassed. His later request to be listened to supports the first reading.

qa.q: What made the difference in the session?
qa.a: Not rushing, offering tissues, and asking what would help gave Santosh control, and he asked to be listened to.

qa.q: How might the volunteer have felt after being asked to sit back?
qa.a: The volunteer probably felt awkward or unsure, having meant to comfort Santosh, and might learn that a cry does not always need fixing.

grounding: Counsellor's note about supporting a crying young adult with tissues, quiet presence and asking what would help, without rushing.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Anjali cried on my bed for an hour tonight. Her research proposal got rejected, the one she's spent eight months on, and her supervisor's email was two lines long.
My first instinct was to say, "Don't cry, it's not the end of the world," because I hate seeing her like that. I actually had my mouth open. Then I remembered how much I hated it when people told me to stop crying after Dadi died. It made my tears feel like a problem to fix.
So I passed her the tissue box and sat on the floor by the bed. After a while I asked, "Do you want me to listen, or distract you, or just be here?" She said, "Just be here. Maybe listen later."
Later she talked for ages. I mostly said "hmm". At the end she hugged me and said it helped.
Gurleen

qa.q: How long had Anjali spent on the research proposal?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: What was Gurleen feeling when about to say 'Don't cry'?
qa.a: Gurleen felt upset and helpless seeing Anjali cry and wanted it to stop, before remembering how hurtful that had felt after Dadi died.

qa.q: Why was Gurleen's question to Anjali helpful?
qa.a: Asking whether Anjali wanted listening, distraction or company let her choose, respecting her control instead of treating the tears as a problem to fix.

qa.q: How did Anjali experience Gurleen's support?
qa.a: Anjali felt comforted enough to talk for ages later and said it helped, because she wasn't rushed or told to stop.

grounding: Shows a young adult resisting the urge to say stop, offering tissues and presence, and asking a crying friend what would help.

passage:
Gurpreet: sorry to message so late. I'm sitting in my car outside the flat crying and I can't make myself go up
Yogesh: hey. no sorry needed. I'm here
Yogesh: do you want to tell me what happened, or should I just keep you company for a bit?
Gurpreet: company. can't type much
Yogesh: ok. no rush. I'll stay on
(a few minutes later)
Gurpreet: they gave my promotion to the new guy. I trained him
Yogesh: that really hurts. of course you're crying
Gurpreet: everyone at work kept saying "don't be upset" like I'm being dramatic
Yogesh: you're not being dramatic. would it help if I came over? I can be there in 15 with chai
Gurpreet: yes please
Yogesh: leaving now. drink some water while you wait?
Gurpreet: ok. thank you 🙏

qa.q: Who got Gurpreet's promotion?
qa.a: The new guy, whom Gurpreet trained.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling in the car?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt hurt and upset, unable to face going up, and also dismissed by colleagues who said 'don't be upset'.

qa.q: How did Yogesh support Gurpreet?
qa.a: Yogesh didn't rush, asked whether Gurpreet wanted to talk or just company, accepted the tears as natural, and offered to come over with chai.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's colleagues have come across by saying 'don't be upset'?
qa.a: They probably meant well but made Gurpreet feel dramatic, as if the tears were the problem rather than the lost promotion.

grounding: Shows a young adult supporting a crying friend by staying present, not rushing, and asking what would help.

passage: The little post office in Bishnupur was about to close when Bidisha saw Leela sitting on the bench outside, crying into the end of her dupatta. The letter in her lap had a government stamp. Bidisha's first impulse was to say, "Arre, stop, people are looking." The postmaster was already peering out. Instead she sat down beside Leela, took a clean handkerchief from her bag, held it out and said nothing for a while. Leela's shoulders shook. A goat cart rattled past. Eventually Bidisha asked softly, "Do you want to tell me, or shall we just sit? Or should I walk you home?" Leela wiped her eyes. "My passport's delayed again. The hospital in Dubai won't hold the job past next month." She cried again, and Bidisha let her. When Leela was ready, Bidisha said, "Tomorrow I'll come with you to the passport office in the district town."

qa.q: Where was the hospital job?
qa.a: In Dubai.

qa.q: What was Bidisha's first impulse, and what does it show she felt?
qa.a: Bidisha felt awkward and self-conscious about people looking, and was tempted to tell Leela to stop.

qa.q: What did Bidisha do instead that helped?
qa.a: She sat beside Leela, offered a handkerchief, stayed quiet, then asked whether Leela wanted to talk, sit or be walked home, and later offered to go with her to the passport office.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Leela to be allowed to cry?
qa.a: Leela could let out her fear and disappointment without feeling rushed or ashamed, which made it easier to explain what was wrong.

grounding: Shows a young adult offering a handkerchief, quiet presence and a choice of help to a crying friend instead of telling her to stop.

passage:
Chen's text said only "can you come over," so Javier cycled across Valencia in the rain. He found Chen at the kitchen table, eyes swollen, a rejection email for the architecture internship still open on the laptop.
Chen started crying again the moment Javier sat down. Javier's first instinct was to say, "Hey, stop, it's just one internship," and he could feel the words on his tongue. He swallowed them. Instead he pushed the tissue box across the table and waited.
It took a while. The rain ticked on the window.
"Sorry," Chen said finally. "I'm being ridiculous."
"You're not. You wanted it." Javier paused. "What would help right now? Food, a walk, or just me being here?"
Chen laughed wetly. "Food. And you being here."
Javier got up to make eggs.

qa.q: What email was open on the laptop?
qa.a: A rejection email for the architecture internship.

qa.q: What was Javier feeling when "stop, it's just one internship" came to mind?
qa.a: Javier likely felt helpless and uncomfortable watching a friend cry and wanted to fix it fast, but he held back.

qa.q: What did Javier offer instead of telling Chen to stop?
qa.a: A tissue box, quiet waiting and a question about what would help: food, a walk or company.

qa.q: How might Chen have felt if Javier had called it just one internship?
qa.a: Chen might have felt dismissed and even more ridiculous, as if wanting the internship didn't matter.

grounding: Supporting a crying friend means offering a tissue and quiet presence, not rushing them, and asking what would help.
